title: Where Did Human Intelligence Come From?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the origins of human intelligence, starting with the split from a common ancestor with chimpanzees six to eight million years ago and the hominin family tree (Ardipithecus, Australopithecus, genus Homo, Homo sapiens). They cover the Upper Paleolithic "big bang" of culture around thirty to sixty thousand years ago, bipedalism and its physical consequences (pelvis, birth canal, Foramen magnum), the brain-size-to-body-size debate, delayed skull fusion and Fontanelles, brain plasticity, the Cosmides and Tooby modular mind theory, the cognitive niche, the role of child-carrying and baby cries and motherese in language, cooking and fire, hunting smaller prey, and the role of language. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Appalachian Trail trail names and hiking experiences.
topics: cooking and fire in human evolution

segments.title: Opening banter and chimp lineage
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on human intelligence and joke about a Simpsons-referencing section title. They explain that humans and chimps share a common ancestor six to eight million years ago and preview the Upper Paleolithic big bang of culture.

segments.title: Hominin family tree and early tool use
segments.summary: The hosts describe the hominin line, Homo sapiens (about three hundred thousand years old), Ardipithecus and Australopithecus, and note that Australopithecus used tools earlier than previously thought. Fire use is dated to at least a million years ago.

segments.title: Bipedalism and physical changes
segments.summary: Walking upright required changes to hind legs, pelvis, and the Foramen magnum. Walking upright saved energy compared with knuckle-walking, and a theory links it to climate change and loss of tree living. Pelvis changes shrank the birth canal.

segments.title: Brain size, birth canal, and delayed skull fusion
segments.summary: Brain-to-body ratios in humans, mice, and elephants show brain size alone does not determine intelligence; connections matter. Smaller birth canals were offset by fontanelles and delayed skull fusion, letting human brains grow after birth.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the plasticity discussion.

segments.title: Brain plasticity and modular mind
segments.summary: Brain plasticity lets the brain rewire with experience, so learning can outpace genetic evolution. Cosmides and Tooby proposed specialized cognitive modules; the hosts discuss cross-referencing between modules, such as following the sunset to following game.

segments.title: Child-rearing, landmarks, motherese, and language
segments.summary: Because mothers could not carry infants while foraging, babies were left behind, favoring spatial mapping memory and baby crying. Motherese, soothing baby talk, may have formed the basis of language.

segments.title: Cognitive niche and tool solutions
segments.summary: The cognitive niche idea holds that intelligence is a general adaptation: tools let humans solve problems like cracking a seed instead of evolving a beak. Solving problems also creates new ones, as with modern petroleum and climate change. Terence McKenna's mushroom theory is mentioned briefly.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short transition break before the cooking discussion.

segments.title: Cooking, hunting smaller prey, and conclusion
segments.summary: Cooking may have unlocked nutrients and calories that fed brain growth. Hunting smaller prey after large animals went extinct may have driven coordination. The hosts conclude language and cooperation tie the theories together, and note that Homo erectus lasted far longer than modern humans.

segments.title: Listener mail: Appalachian Trail
segments.summary: Listener Sophie, trail name Tough Cookie, describes her thru-hike with her sister, trail names, and trail magic, and invites the hosts to Kentucky.
